draft.title: Conjectures and if and only if
card: A conjecture is a statement that is believed true but is not yet proved. It stays a conjecture until it is proved or disproved.
P ⇒ Q means if P is true, then Q is true. We say P is sufficient for Q, and Q is necessary for P.
P ⇔ Q means P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P. Read it as P if and only if Q. Each side is both necessary and sufficient for the other.

To prove P ⇔ Q, prove both directions. Example: n is even ⇔ n² is even. The 'n is even ⇒ n² is even' direction is true, but 'n² is even ⇒ n is even' must also be shown. Here both hold, so the ⇔ is true. For x > 2 ⇒ x² > 4, the reverse fails at x = −3, so ⇔ is false.
draft.remember: P ⇔ Q needs both P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P to be true.

a.q: Which is needed to prove the statement P ⇔ Q?
opts: P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P are both proved
P ⇒ Q is proved for several cases
Q ⇒ P is proved for several cases
P ⇒ Q is proved and Q is checked once
a.why: ⇔ means each side implies the other, so both directions must be proved. Proving only P ⇒ Q shows P is sufficient for Q, but not that Q is sufficient for P.
a.clue: Think of the two arrows inside ⇔.

b.q: For a real number x, consider: x = 3 ⇒ x² = 9. Which statement about it is correct?
opts: x = 3 is sufficient but not necessary for x² = 9
x = 3 is necessary but not sufficient for x² = 9
x = 3 is both necessary and sufficient for x² = 9
x = 3 is neither necessary nor sufficient for x² = 9
b.why: If x = 3 then x² = 9, so x = 3 is sufficient. But x = −3 also gives x² = 9, so x = 3 is not necessary. The reverse implication fails, so the ⇔ is false.

a.best: P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P are both proved

b.best: x = 3 is sufficient but not necessary for x² = 9
